items.prompt: In basic breath awareness meditation, what is the usual object of attention?

options.label: A detailed picture of a peaceful place
The natural sensations of breathing
A running count of your passing thoughts
A mantra repeated aloud in rhythm

rubric: Breath awareness anchors attention on the sensations of the natural breath.
Distractors confuse it with mantra or visualisation practices.

items.prompt: What does a body scan involve?

options.label: Checking posture and correcting it constantly
Imagining a light that heals each organ
Tensing each muscle as hard as possible
Moving attention through body parts, noticing sensations

rubric: A body scan moves attention gradually through the body to notice sensations.
Distractors describe progressive muscle relaxation, visualisation or posture correction.

items.prompt: Which silent phrase is typical of loving-kindness (metta) meditation?

options.label: "Scan from head to toe"
"May you be happy and safe"
"Let every thought pass by"
"Breathe in, breathe out"

rubric: Loving-kindness uses phrases that wish wellbeing to oneself and others.
Other options are instructions from open monitoring, breath awareness and body scan.

items.prompt: What does the abbreviation MBSR stand for?

options.label: Meditative Breath Support Recovery
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction
Mind-Body Sleep Routine
Mindful Behaviour Self-Regulation

rubric: MBSR is Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, the eight-week programme developed by Jon Kabat-Zinn.
Distractors are plausible but invented expansions.

items.prompt: Which term names the practice of noticing whatever arises (sounds, thoughts, sensations) without focusing on one chosen object?

options.label: Breath counting
Mantra repetition
Focused concentration
Open monitoring

rubric: Open monitoring means widely noticing experience as it arises.
Other options all fix attention on a single object.

items.prompt: Which of the following are core mindfulness and meditation practices? Select all that apply.

options.label: Speed reading drills
Memorising long texts
Body scan
Loving-kindness
Breath awareness

rubric: Breath awareness, body scan and loving-kindness are core practices.
Speed reading and memorisation are attention-related skills but not meditation practices.

items.prompt: A beginner is following the instruction to focus on the breath at the nostrils. After a minute they realise they have been thinking about dinner. According to the standard instruction, what is the next step?

options.label: Gently return attention to the breath
Push the thought away by force of will
Keep thinking until the thought finishes
Stop and restart the session from the beginning

rubric: The standard instruction is to notice the wandering and gently return to the breath.
Distractors reflect restarting, indulging or forcefully suppressing thoughts.

items.prompt: During breath meditation, a learner's mind wanders many times and they feel they are failing. How should this be understood?

options.label: It means they should breathe more deeply so the breath becomes easier to hold attention on
It shows meditation is not working for them, since a trained mind would stay on the breath
Noticing the wandering is itself the moment of awareness being trained
It means they need to switch to a longer session so the mind has time to settle down

rubric: Noticing wandering and returning is the core repetition that builds attention.
Distractors treat wandering as failure that needs fixing.

items.prompt: How does open monitoring differ from breath awareness?

options.label: It is practised only while lying down, never seated
It focuses on a repeated phrase instead of the breath
It still follows the breath but with the eyes closed
It has no single anchor and notices whatever arises

rubric: Open monitoring lacks a single anchor, unlike breath awareness.
Distractors suggest superficial differences such as posture or a mantra.

items.prompt: Why is a body scan often used to manage stress?

options.label: It trains muscles to stay relaxed throughout the day
It helps you notice tension early, before it builds
It distracts you from unpleasant feelings and thoughts
It replaces the need to rest or sleep at night

rubric: Body scans train awareness of bodily sensations, so tension is noticed sooner.
Distractors see it as forced relaxation, distraction or a substitute for rest.

items.prompt: What is a realistic expectation after several weeks of 10 minutes of daily mindfulness practice?

options.label: Attention can stay on one demanding task for several hours without drifting
Stressful events still occur but no longer cause any bodily or emotional reaction
Thoughts stop appearing during sitting once the breath is followed steadily
Distraction is noticed sooner, though thoughts still arise

rubric: Practice improves noticing of distraction; it does not remove thoughts or reactions.
Distractors promise unrealistic total outcomes.

items.prompt: In mindfulness, what does "non-judgmental" awareness mean?

options.label: Noticing experience without labelling it good or bad
Approving of every experience you have, even painful ones
Avoiding decisions so that you never have to evaluate
Not caring how things turn out in your own life

rubric: Non-judgmental means observing without automatic evaluation or reaction.
Distractors confuse it with apathy, approval or passivity.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain mindfulness practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: The aim is to empty the mind of all thoughts
Loving-kindness cultivates warmth toward self and others
It trains attention to the present moment
Strong emotions mean the practice has failed

rubric: Mindfulness trains present-moment attention and loving-kindness cultivates goodwill.
Emptying the mind and viewing emotions as failure are common misconceptions.

items.prompt: Before a big meeting, Sam feels anxious and takes three minutes to notice the breath and where the anxiety sits in the body. Sam does not try to remove the feeling. What is this practice most likely doing for Sam?

options.label: Helping Sam notice anxiety without being swept along by it
Proving to Sam that the meeting is not worth worrying about
Replacing the preparation Sam would otherwise do for the meeting
Gradually shrinking the anxiety until it stops coming back

rubric: Observing anxiety with awareness creates space between feeling and reaction.
Distractors assume mindfulness eliminates feelings or substitutes for action.

items.prompt: During breath awareness, your mind wanders to a to-do list and you notice it. What does that moment of noticing represent?

options.label: A lapse that shows your concentration is poor and must be fixed before you continue
A core part of the practice, since noticing and returning builds attention
A signal to stop and restart the session once your mind has become clearer
Proof that you need to suppress thoughts more firmly the next time you sit

rubric: Noticing wandering and gently returning is the repeated skill being trained.
Distractors treat wandering as failure or call for suppression, which misreads the practice.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes what a body scan is?

options.label: A method for forcing every muscle to relax completely within ten minutes
Moving attention slowly through body regions to notice sensations as they are
A visualisation of healing light that removes illness from each body part
A medical check where you diagnose problems in each part of your body

rubric: A body scan is systematic attention to sensations without trying to change them.
Distractors confuse it with forced relaxation, healing imagery or self-diagnosis.

items.prompt: A learner sits and simply notices whatever arises, such as sounds, thoughts and sensations, without holding onto one anchor. Which practice is this?

options.label: Focused attention on the breath, because breathing is always present
Open monitoring, because awareness stays wide with no single chosen object
A body scan, because sensations are among the things being noticed
Loving-kindness meditation, because it welcomes everything that arises

rubric: Open monitoring means broad, receptive awareness without a fixed anchor.
Distractors name practices that use a specific object or phrases as the focus.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of silently repeating phrases such as 'may you be well' in loving-kindness practice?

options.label: To practise open monitoring by observing how each phrase feels
To cultivate warm goodwill toward yourself and others through repetition
To block out distracting thoughts by keeping the mind busy with words
To predict and secure good outcomes for the people you name

rubric: The phrases are used to cultivate goodwill as a trained attitude.
Distractors treat them as thought-blocking, a wish that controls outcomes, or open monitoring.

items.prompt: A beginner believes good meditation means a perfectly empty mind. What is the most likely result of this belief?

options.label: They will see no effect, since beliefs do not alter how practice feels
They will mostly judge sessions as failures because thoughts keep arising
They will quickly reach stillness since expectation focuses attention
They will find thoughts fade, because wanting emptiness weakens them

rubric: Thoughts naturally arise, so expecting emptiness leads to self-criticism.
Distractors assume expectation produces stillness or has no effect.

items.prompt: Which of the following describe the attitude usually encouraged in mindfulness practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Striving to reach a special calm state every session
Non-judging awareness of experience as it is
Curiosity about sensations, thoughts and emotions
Pushing unpleasant feelings out of awareness quickly
Patience when attention wanders repeatedly

rubric: Non-judging, curiosity and patience are core attitudes.
Suppressing feelings and striving for a particular state run against acceptance.

items.prompt: Maya lies down for a 20-minute body scan after work. By the time she reaches her legs she has drifted into sleep twice. She concludes she is bad at meditation. Which interpretation best fits mindfulness teaching?

options.label: Sleepiness shows she failed to concentrate and should try harder to force alertness
Sleepiness means the body scan is unsuitable for her and she should quit it
Sleepiness is common lying down and can be noticed, with posture or timing adjusted
Sleepiness proves she reached deep relaxation, which is the goal of the scan

rubric: Drowsiness is common in the lying posture and is handled by noticing and adjusting.
Distractors call it failure, a reason to quit, or the goal itself.

items.prompt: You are counting breaths from one to ten and realise you have been planning dinner for a while. What is the best next step?

options.label: Mentally scold yourself, then resume counting at the highest number
Follow the dinner plan until it is complete, then go back to the breath
Notice the planning without judgement and return to counting from one
Restart the whole session after clearing your mind of dinner thoughts

rubric: Noticing kindly and returning to the anchor is the standard step.
Distractors add self-criticism, restarting or following the thought.

items.prompt: In a body scan you have just finished attending to your left foot. Following the usual progressive order, where does your attention go next?

options.label: The top of the head, to jump to the opposite end
The chest, because the heart is the main body centre
The left ankle and lower leg, moving gradually upward
The right hand, to alternate sides of the body

rubric: Body scans usually move progressively through adjacent regions.
Distractors skip around the body and break the systematic sequence.

items.prompt: You have three minutes before a tense meeting and your mind is racing. Which short practice fits best?

options.label: A full-length body scan, hurrying through each region in turn
Focused attention on the breath, feeling the sensation of each exhale
Open monitoring of every thought that arises for the full time
Three minutes of loving-kindness phrases for everyone in the meeting

rubric: A short anchor on breath sensations steadies racing attention quickly.
Distractors need more time or give a racing mind too little to hold.

items.prompt: A learner begins loving-kindness by sending phrases to a person they are in conflict with and feels tense and overwhelmed. What adjustment applies the practice best?

options.label: Skip loving-kindness and switch to counting breaths permanently
Begin with easier recipients such as yourself or a close friend
Repeat the phrases faster so the negative feelings have less time
Keep going with the difficult person until the tension passes

rubric: The practice is usually built gradually, starting with easier recipients.
Distractors force through, abandon the practice or rush it.

items.prompt: You want a steady daily practice but keep forgetting to meditate. Which plan is most likely to work?

options.label: Do five minutes right after your morning coffee each day
Meditate whenever you feel stressed enough to remember it
Wait for a free weekend and do one long session then
Set a goal of sixty minutes daily so it feels important

rubric: Short sessions tied to an existing routine build habit.
Distractors rely on mood, rare long sessions or an unrealistic goal.

items.prompt: During sitting meditation a dull ache grows in your knee. Which responses fit mindfulness practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Conclude that meditation is harmful and stop for good
Adjust your posture mindfully and carry on with the practice
Clench against it and sit still no matter how severe it becomes
Explore the ache with curiosity, noticing how its quality shifts

rubric: Exploring mild discomfort and mindfully adjusting posture are both appropriate.
Gritting through severe pain or quitting entirely are not.

items.prompt: Leo opens an email from his manager criticising his report and feels his chest tighten and his thoughts speed up. He wants to apply mindfulness before replying. Which sequence best applies it?

options.label: Spend the afternoon replaying the email to understand why it hurt
Push the tension aside and focus on drafting the perfect answer
Pause, take a few breaths, notice body sensations, then choose a reply
Reply immediately while the feelings are fresh to stay honest

rubric: Pausing, breathing and noticing the body creates space before responding.
Distractors act on impulse, suppress feelings or ruminate.

items.prompt: You are counting breaths from 1 to 10. Partway through you realise you are at "23" and have been planning dinner. What do you do next?

options.label: Note the drift without judgment and begin again at 1
Continue counting from 24 so the session total stays accurate
Stop the session because your focus is clearly too poor today
Analyse the dinner plan until the thought settles, then resume

rubric: Breath counting restarts at 1 after a lapse, and the gentle return is the training.
Distractors treat the lapse as failure or as something to resolve before returning.

items.prompt: You are guiding yourself through a 20-minute body scan lying down. Which approach fits the practice?

options.label: Jump between regions at random to keep the mind from getting bored
Move from the toes upward region by region, noticing sensations as they are
Tense each region hard and then release it to produce deep relaxation
Skip any region that feels painful so the scan stays pleasant

rubric: A body scan moves systematically through the body, observing sensations without trying to change them.
Distractors confuse it with progressive muscle relaxation or with avoidance.

items.prompt: In a loving-kindness session you have sent phrases to yourself, a close friend and a neutral acquaintance such as a cashier. Following the traditional sequence, whom do you direct them to next?

options.label: A person you find difficult
All beings everywhere
A second close friend
Yourself again, for a full round

rubric: The traditional order is self, loved one, neutral person, difficult person, then all beings.
Jumping to all beings skips the difficult person step.

items.prompt: During open monitoring practice, a car alarm starts outside. Which response applies the technique?

options.label: Return to a single anchor like the breath and push the sound out of awareness
Note "hearing" as it arises, then let it pass without chasing it
Work out where the alarm is and whether it is yours, then settle again
Open your eyes and end the session until the noise has stopped for good

rubric: Open monitoring treats sounds as experiences to notice and release.
Distractors narrow attention, which is the focused-attention style, or react to the content.

items.prompt: You are new to meditation and have about five spare minutes a day. Which plan best applies habit-building principles?

options.label: Sit for 40 minutes on weekends, when you have more free time to settle in
Start with 30 minutes daily so you see quick results and stay motivated
Meditate whenever you feel stressed enough to need it, so practice stays purposeful
Sit five minutes right after brushing your teeth each morning

rubric: A short, regular session tied to an existing habit builds steadiness.
Distractors rely on motivation, irregular timing or an unsustainable length.

items.prompt: During breath awareness you notice your mind has wandered into a memory. Which responses apply the practice correctly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Gently guide attention back to the breath
Scold yourself so you are less likely to drift again
Silently label it "thinking"
Restart the whole session from the beginning
Remind yourself that wandering is normal and expected

rubric: Noticing, labelling and returning gently is the repeated core move.
Restarting or scolding treats wandering as a mistake rather than as part of training.

items.prompt: Marta feels anxious before presenting and has three minutes in a quiet corridor. She has learned breath awareness and body scans. Which use of those three minutes best applies her skills?

options.label: Observe each worry openly and analyse it until she has solved it before she walks into the room
Try to empty her mind of every thought about the presentation before she walks in
Rest attention on breath and feet, returning each time she drifts to the talk
Do a rapid full-body scan, spending a few seconds on each region from head to toe

rubric: A short anchored practice steadies attention in the present, and wandering is simply met by returning.
Distractors aim at thought suppression, an unrealistically rushed scan or problem-solving rumination.

items.prompt: Sam practises a lying body scan right after lunch and keeps falling asleep. Which analysis of the cause and adjustment is most sound?

options.label: Posture and timing favour drowsiness, so sit upright or practise earlier
The scan technique is flawed, so he should switch to loving-kindness
His attention is too weak, so he should force harder concentration
Falling asleep shows deep relaxation, so no change is needed

rubric: Lying down after a meal predisposes drowsiness, so posture and timing are the likely causes.
Distractors blame the technique or effort or treat sleep as the aim.

items.prompt: During loving-kindness practice, Ana directs phrases at a coworker who recently humiliated her and feels only anger. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The target is too difficult this early, so she should start with easier recipients
The practice is not suited to her temperament, so she should switch to breath awareness for good
The anger shows the phrases are insincere, so she should repeat them more forcefully until warmth arises
The anger is a distraction unrelated to the practice, so she should note it and keep to the phrases

rubric: Starting with a strongly charged person overreaches, and stepping back to easier recipients is the usual adjustment.
Distractors read the anger as failure, force the phrases or deny its relevance.

items.prompt: Which statement best captures how focused attention on the breath differs structurally from open monitoring?

options.label: Focused attention is for beginners only, while open monitoring is only for experts
Focused attention suppresses thoughts, while open monitoring encourages following them
Focused attention uses the body, while open monitoring uses only thoughts
Focused attention keeps one chosen anchor, while open monitoring tracks whatever arises

rubric: The difference lies in the attentional structure: a fixed object versus a receptive field.
Distractors misdescribe suppression, expertise or the objects of attention.

items.prompt: Lee says, "I'm failing at meditation because my mind never stops thinking." Which flaw in this reasoning matters most?

options.label: It overlooks that he needs a quieter room before any real progress is possible
It assumes the goal is no thoughts, when noticing and returning is the exercise
It overlooks that thoughts should be analysed in depth until they finally stop
It confuses meditation with relaxation, so he should aim for a drowsy, calm state

rubric: Thought is normal, and each noticing of it is a repetition of the skill.
Distractors keep the false premise that a quiet mind is the criterion.

items.prompt: Priya becomes more tense during breath meditation and notices she is trying to make each breath slow and perfect. What is the likely cause?

options.label: Her natural breathing rate is too fast, so she needs to train it slower first
She is sitting for too short a time, so the calming effect has not yet begun
She is controlling the breath instead of simply observing it
She has picked an anchor that suits her poorly, so she should switch to sound

rubric: Manipulating the breath adds effort and monitoring tension, whereas the instruction is to observe it as it is.
Distractors blame breathing speed, duration or anchor choice.

items.prompt: A learner doing open monitoring may slip into rumination. Which observations suggest this has happened? Select all that apply.

options.label: Feeling the same worry repeat with growing tension
Hearing a bird and then noticing the next sound
Judging themselves as a bad meditator and replaying it
Noticing a thought, labelling it, and letting it fade
Following a chain of thoughts about a past argument for minutes

rubric: Rumination shows as sustained narrative, self-judgment and repetition with tension.
Labelling thoughts and moving on to the next experience are signs of open monitoring.

items.prompt: Jo has meditated 10 minutes daily for three weeks and finds sessions calm. Yet in tense team meetings she still reacts sharply. She only ever practises alone at home with her eyes closed. What is the best analysis?

options.label: Her sessions are too short for lasting change, so only about an hour a day would shift how she behaves in meetings
Her technique is wrong, because sessions that feel calm show she is avoiding discomfort rather than observing it
Her skill has not transferred to live situations, so brief informal moments in meetings could bridge it
Three weeks is too soon for any carry-over, so no change in meetings can be expected until a year of practice

rubric: Skills practised only in calm settings often need cued, brief use in real situations to generalise.
Distractors blame length, technique or a fixed timeline instead of the transfer gap.

items.prompt: A learner doing breath awareness says their chest tightens and they feel anxious each time they focus on the breath. They admit they keep trying to make the breath deeper and more even. Which diagnosis best explains the anxiety?

options.label: Breath awareness is unsuitable for anyone with anxious tendencies, so another practice is always needed.
They are managing the breath instead of observing it, which turns the anchor into a performance task.
Anxiety during practice shows the learner is concentrating too weakly to hold the breath as an anchor.
Focusing on the breath always raises arousal at first, and this effect fades only if they push through.

rubric: Controlling the breath converts observation into effortful regulation, which can raise tension.
Distractors treat the anxiety as a blanket contraindication or as a concentration deficit.

items.prompt: A learner practices a lying-down body scan at 10 pm after a long day and falls asleep within minutes almost every time. What is the most defensible analysis?

options.label: Falling asleep shows the scan is working as intended, because deep relaxation is the main aim of the practice and the learner should keep the routine.
The learner probably lacks the concentration needed for body scans, so they should switch to a different practice until their attention has improved.
Lying down at a low-energy time lowers alertness, so the drowsiness reflects the conditions, not the technique.
Body scans tend to induce sleep in most people, so they are a poor way to train attention at any time of day, whatever the posture.

rubric: Posture and timing lower arousal; changing them tests the cause.
Distractors mistake sleep for success or blame an inability, ignoring the conditions.

items.prompt: After eight weeks of open monitoring, two learners report. Ana says she has far fewer thoughts. Ben says he still drifts into stories but notices within seconds instead of minutes. Which report better indicates skill development?

options.label: Neither, since progress can only be judged by an instructor and not by a learner's own reports.
Ben's, since a shorter lag before noticing drift reflects improved meta-awareness, whatever the thought count.
Ana's, since a quieter mind shows stronger concentration and is the main sign of progress.
Both equally, since any change in the number of thoughts or in awareness counts as the same progress.

rubric: The trained skill is noticing mental activity sooner, not suppressing it.
Ana's report fits the common misconception that meditation means having fewer thoughts.

items.prompt: In a first loving-kindness session, a learner begins by sending phrases to a coworker they dislike and ends up feeling irritated and tense. Which step in their approach most likely caused the problem?

options.label: They repeated the phrases silently rather than aloud, which weakens the emotional effect of the practice.
They used phrases at all, since loving-kindness works only through imagery and never through words.
They practiced with eyes closed, which always amplifies negative feelings toward other people.
They started with a difficult person instead of building up gradually from oneself or a benefactor.

rubric: Traditional sequencing builds goodwill with easier targets before a difficult person.
Distractors blame incidental features of delivery that do not explain the irritation.

items.prompt: During a session a car alarm sounds outside. Comparing focused attention on the breath with open monitoring, how does each practice treat the alarm?

options.label: Both treat it as a distraction to be shut out, then return attention firmly to the breath each time.
Neither addresses outside sounds, so the learner should stop and relocate to a silent room before continuing.
Focused attention takes the alarm as the main object of awareness, while open monitoring returns to the breath.
Focused attention notes it and returns to the breath; open monitoring takes it as one more object to observe.

rubric: Focused attention keeps a single anchor; open monitoring has no fixed anchor.
Distractors blur the two styles or reverse their handling of sound.

items.prompt: A participant on a long silent retreat reports growing distress after several days of eight-hour practice days. Which factors could plausibly contribute? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reading the distress as proof of failing may lead them to fight it and escalate it.
Long sessions with little pacing or teacher check-in can intensify difficult experiences.
Suppressed painful material may surface without the support to work through it.
Slow breathing is toxic when sustained over many hours and causes the distress directly.
Silence by itself depletes the brain's attention capacity until anxiety appears in all people.

rubric: Intensity, surfacing material and a self-critical stance are recognised contributors to difficult experiences.
The other options assert unsupported mechanisms.

items.prompt: A manager meditates 20 minutes every morning in a quiet room and enjoys it. Yet in tense meetings she still reacts sharply and only realises afterwards. She has never tried the practice outside the cushion. What best explains the gap?

options.label: Her practice only occurs in low-demand conditions, so noticing is untrained at moments of high stress.
She enjoys the sessions too much, and enjoyment prevents the discomfort that is needed for learning.
Twenty minutes is too short to affect behaviour, so the practice must be doubled before any change appears.
Meditation cannot influence workplace reactions, which are fixed traits beyond the reach of attention training.

rubric: Skill transfer needs practice at triggers, such as brief pauses in real situations.
Distractors blame duration or enjoyment or treat reactions as fixed.

items.prompt: Criteria: five minutes, a shared open-plan office, no privacy, and a need to settle nerves before a presentation. Which option best fits?

options.label: A 20-minute lying body scan on the floor of a nearby meeting room.
A full open-monitoring sit with eyes closed until the mind stops producing thoughts.
A loving-kindness session aloud toward each colleague who might judge the presentation.
Eyes-open breath awareness with attention on breath and feet contact for a few minutes.

rubric: A brief, discreet, open-eyed anchor fits time and privacy limits.
The other options violate the time, privacy or realistic-aim criteria.

items.prompt: A person with chronic pain wants to lessen their distress about it, not to eliminate the pain. Which instruction best meets this goal?

options.label: Hold rigid stillness and push through the intensity until the pain fades by sheer endurance.
Imagine the painful area as pain-free so that the sensations are replaced by calm imagery.
Notice the sensations as changing heat or pressure, and notice the urge to resist them.
Return to the breath whenever pain arises, so that attention rests on a neutral anchor instead.

rubric: Observing sensations and resistance separately targets suffering rather than pain intensity.
Distractors rely on endurance, avoidance or imagery that denies the sensations.

items.prompt: Criteria: a working parent with unpredictable days wants a practice that is still running after eight weeks. Which plan is the strongest?

options.label: Eight minutes daily tied to an existing routine like the first coffee, with a two-minute fallback.
Daily sits at whatever time feels right, with no fixed cue, to keep the practice spontaneous.
An hour each morning for two weeks, then stopping to judge whether the effects were worth it.
One 30-minute sit each weekend, since longer sessions yield more benefit than short ones.

rubric: Cue-linked short sessions with a fallback maximise consistency under variable schedules.
Distractors favour duration or spontaneity over adherence.

items.prompt: A teacher leads loving-kindness for a group that includes someone recently bereaved. Criterion: minimise the risk of overwhelming people while keeping the practice useful. Which adaptation is best?

options.label: Skip the session, since loving-kindness is unsafe for anyone who has experienced any loss.
Direct everyone toward the deceased person first, because grief is best met immediately and fully.
Offer self-directed or benefactor phrases first, and invite participants to pause or change target as needed.
Require everyone to complete the full sequence including difficult people, to keep the group uniform.

rubric: Choice of target and permission to stop reduce overwhelm while retaining the practice.
Distractors force exposure, enforce uniformity, or overgeneralise the risk.

items.prompt: A restless adult who struggles to sit still wants to train attention. Criteria: keep them practicing and build sustained focus gradually. Which plan is best?

options.label: Begin with open monitoring only, since a fixed anchor would feel too restrictive for them.
Short sits plus walking meditation, lengthening the sits slowly as comfort and focus grow.
Delay all practice until restlessness has gone away by itself through other means.
One 40-minute seated session daily, to force the mind to settle quickly.

rubric: Short, varied sessions with a gradual progression support adherence and attention building.
Distractors demand tolerance beyond their current capacity or postpone the practice.

items.prompt: A workplace wants to judge whether its meditation course helps people manage stress. Which are sound criteria for judging this? Select all that apply.

options.label: How many minutes of thought-free calm each person reports during sessions.
Whether practice logs agree with self-reported reactivity over several weeks.
Whether people notice stress reactions earlier and recover from them more quickly.
Whether participants use brief practices at real triggers, not only in sessions.
How blissful participants say the sessions felt on a given day.

rubric: Sound criteria look at real-world reactivity, transfer and consistent evidence over time.
Thought-free minutes and bliss reflect common misconceptions about what the practice aims for.

items.prompt: After six weeks of body scans, a student feels bored and wants to switch to a different technique whenever boredom appears. The goal is stable attention. Which advice is best?

options.label: Observe the boredom itself for a few sessions before switching, so the switch is a choice, not an escape.
Switch at once whenever boredom arises, since boredom shows the technique has stopped being useful.
Double the session length so that boredom is overcome through sheer effort and willpower.
Stop meditating until motivation returns, because practice done while bored builds bad habits.

rubric: Treating boredom as an object of observation builds stability; switching reflexively reinforces avoidance.
Distractors escape the feeling, stop practice, or rely on force.

items.prompt: A participant with a trauma history says body scans leave her feeling flooded and detached. Criteria: keep her safe, preserve her access to the practice, and respect her agency. Which adjustment is best?

options.label: Remove her from the course, since body-focused practices are unsafe for anyone with any trauma history at all
Ask her to stay with the sensations through to the end, since sustained exposure in silence will reduce the flooding
Keep the scan unchanged but lengthen it, since more sustained practice gives faster habituation to intense feelings
Offer choice: eyes open, attention on her feet or on sounds as an anchor, and permission to stop or skip regions

rubric: Choice, an external anchor and the option to stop keep her within a tolerable window while preserving the practice.
Distractors treat forced exposure or total avoidance as the answer, ignoring graded, agency-respecting adaptation.

items.prompt: A teacher tells students: 'Count breaths to ten. Every time you lose count, you have failed; restart at one and be stricter with yourself next time.' Judged against how mindfulness training works, which critique is strongest?

options.label: It is sound, because strict penalties train concentration faster and reduce wandering through consistent negative feedback
It misframes the rep: noticing a lapse and returning gently is the skill, and harshness builds aversion to practice
It is flawed because lost counts show the technique is wrong, so students should switch to a different anchor at once
It is flawed only because counting is too advanced, so students should drop the anchor and follow their thoughts freely

rubric: Noticing wandering and returning is the core repetition; self-punishment undermines the attitude of kindness and sustainability.
Distractors either endorse harshness or blame the anchor, missing that lapses are part of the training.

items.prompt: A study reports that adults who completed an 8-week mindfulness course had lower stress than a waitlist group. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: Mindfulness works better than other stress treatments such as exercise or therapy, since it beat the comparison group
The result is uninterpretable, because any waitlist comparison is invalid and cannot show benefit of any course
Meditation itself is the active ingredient, because the two groups differed in whether they learned to meditate at all
The course beat doing nothing, but the design cannot separate meditation from expectancy, group contact or teacher attention

rubric: A waitlist control shows the package helped versus nothing but cannot isolate specific ingredients.
Distractors overclaim specificity or superiority, or wrongly dismiss waitlist designs entirely.

items.prompt: A self-critical learner starts loving-kindness with 'May I be happy' and feels only irritation and guilt. Criteria: keep the practice workable and build genuine goodwill. Which revision is best?

options.label: Drop all warm-hearted practice for good and use only breath focus, since self-criticism rules out these practices
Repeat the self-directed phrases louder and more often, since irritation signals resistance that repetition will overcome
Start with someone they actively dislike, since the strongest resistance produces the fastest growth in compassion
Begin with an easy recipient such as a mentor or pet, use phrases that feel true, and approach the self gradually

rubric: Starting with an easy recipient and believable phrases builds real goodwill that can later extend to the self.
Distractors force the hard step, choose the hardest recipient first, or abandon the practice.

items.prompt: A retreat organiser must rank screening concerns for ten days of silent, intensive practice. Which applicant most needs individual assessment before acceptance, judged by risk of serious harm?

options.label: Someone with sore knees who must use a chair and expects to feel physically uncomfortable during long sittings
Someone who drinks many coffees daily and expects headaches from caffeine withdrawal and disrupted sleep early on
Someone recovering from a recent psychotic episode, with recent medication changes and thin support at home
Someone who has never meditated before and is anxious about enduring ten days of silence with no talking

rubric: Intensive silent practice can destabilise people with recent psychosis, so this carries the highest risk.
Distractors are discomforts or nerves that are manageable and not serious risks.

items.prompt: Which are sound criteria for judging whether a six-month daily practice is working? Select all that apply.

options.label: Returning to practice after missed days without self-punishment
Bringing the same noticing into everyday stress, such as meetings
Noticing thoughts and emotions sooner, before they drive reactions
Feeling calm and blissful in every sitting
Sessions rarely containing any wandering thoughts

rubric: Earlier noticing, kind resumption and transfer to daily life reflect real skill change.
Absence of thoughts and constant bliss are common misconceptions about what progress looks like.

items.prompt: An employee in a workplace mindfulness program reports that after three weeks she feels more stressed and keeps noticing tension she previously ignored. She still sits 10 minutes daily. Which evaluation of her situation is best?

options.label: The practice is clearly harming her, so she should stop immediately and avoid mindfulness training altogether from now on
Her stress shows she needs more time, so she should triple her daily sitting and push through the discomfort
Awareness of existing stress often rises early; keep sessions short, use an anchor, and address workload causes as well
She is doing it wrong by noticing tension, so she should aim to empty her mind and stop attending to her body

rubric: Early rise in noticed stress is common; supportive adjustment plus tackling the real stressors is balanced.
Distractors overreact by quitting, misread the aim as emptiness, or escalate dose without support.

items.prompt: Design a 4-week plan for a nurse with only 5-minute pockets, no quiet space and exhaustion after shifts. Constraints: daily, low effort, skills build gradually. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: Commit to a 45-minute sit each morning before shifts, since longer sessions always build skill faster than short ones
Tie a 5-minute breath anchor to a fixed cue daily, add mindful handwashing on shifts, and add 2 minutes each week
Use random app reminders for 20-minute guided sessions, relying on prompts and willpower instead of a fixed daily cue
Do one long body scan each weekend and nothing on workdays, since weekdays are too busy to practise at all

rubric: Short, cue-linked practice plus informal moments and gradual extension fits all constraints.
Distractors ignore time, daily frequency or habit cues.

items.prompt: Design a body scan for a person with chronic back pain. Constraints: avoid fixating on the pain, keep curiosity about sensation, and keep the user in control. Which design fits?

options.label: Skip every painful area and scan only pain-free regions, so attention never touches the discomfort at any point
Visit all regions, alternate painful and neutral areas, and let the user skip any region
Guide a fast, uniform scan with commands to relax each region, so tension is released on instruction in every part
Concentrate the whole scan on the painful area until the sensation fades, so the pain is fully resolved by the end

rubric: Alternating pain and neutral areas with user choice prevents fixation while keeping curiosity.
Distractors fixate, avoid entirely, or demand relaxation, each violating a constraint.

items.prompt: Design the order of a four-week introductory course. Constraints: stable attention before wide awareness, some warmth practice early to offset self-criticism, each skill builds on the last. Which sequence fits?

options.label: Loving-kindness only in week one, then drop it and teach breath anchoring and body scan with no open awareness
Breath anchoring, then body scan, then open monitoring, with short loving-kindness closings added from week two
Open monitoring in week one, then breath anchoring, then body scan, with no warmth practice until the course ends
Body scan, then open monitoring, then breath anchoring, with warmth practice left as optional homework at the end

rubric: Anchor first, then body awareness, then open monitoring, with early warmth, meets every constraint.
Distractors put wide awareness before stable attention or omit early warmth.

items.prompt: A school proposes 10 minutes of silent meditation daily for all pupils, led by a teacher after a one-hour webinar, with no opt-out. Criteria: safety and sustainability. Which missing element matters most?

options.label: A longer 30-minute session, since 10 minutes is too short to produce any measurable effect on pupils
Trained teachers with their own practice, plus choice to adapt or opt out for pupils who find it distressing
A requirement that pupils sit cross-legged and silent, since strict posture ensures proper technique and seriousness
A grading system for meditation quality, since marks motivate pupils to practise more carefully and consistently

rubric: Teacher competence and pupil choice address safety and sustainability directly.
Distractors add length, rigidity or grading, which increase pressure rather than safety.

items.prompt: Design a 5-minute response to a strong craving (for example to smoke). Constraints: do not suppress it, do not act on it automatically, use a body anchor. Which protocol fits?

options.label: Tighten every muscle and hold the breath to prove the urge is controllable, then resume the day as normal
Name the urge, find it in the body, watch it rise, peak and fall with the breath, then choose the next action
Give in to the craving mindfully, noticing each sensation as you act, and reflect afterwards so the urge is met without guilt
Push the urge out of mind by firmly thinking of something else, so it has no chance to build up and take hold

rubric: Naming, locating and observing the urge's wave meets all three constraints.
Distractors suppress, act automatically, or use forceful control.

items.prompt: Design a 20-minute session for mixed beginners. Constraints: anchor attention, normalise wandering, avoid overwhelm. Which components fit? Select all that apply.

options.label: Guidance that wandering is normal and returning is the practice
An eyes-open option and a brief transition back to activity at the end
Fifteen minutes of unguided silence with no instruction
An instruction to stop all thoughts before the bell
A clear anchor such as breath at the nostrils or belly

rubric: An anchor, normalising wandering and gentle options with a transition meet the constraints.
Long unguided silence and thought-stopping overwhelm beginners and misstate the aim.

items.prompt: A practitioner has sat 25 minutes each morning for three years and now fights drowsiness and dull wandering. Constraints: keep the morning slot, stay awake, keep it meditation rather than a nap. Which redesign fits best?

options.label: Lie down and run a long body scan, since lying relaxed keeps attention steady and avoids tension in the body
Close the eyes, soften all effort, and let the mind drift freely, since forcing alertness is what causes drowsiness
Shorten the sitting to five minutes and add a cup of coffee, ignoring posture and technique in the practice
Sit upright with eyes open, start with brisk counting or noting, then move to open monitoring once alert

rubric: Upright posture, open eyes and an energetic start counter drowsiness while keeping real practice.
Distractors encourage lying down, drifting or abandoning technique, which feed drowsiness.
